name: Graham Net-Nets (NCAV)
src: Benjamin Graham and David Dodd, 'Security Analysis' (1934); Graham, 'The Intelligent Investor' (1949)
thesis: Buy companies below liquidation value: price under two-thirds of net current asset value is a statistical bargain basket.
criteria: NCAV = current assets - total liabilities (and preferred stock)
Buy at price < 2/3 x NCAV per share
Diversify widely; Oppenheimer's test re-formed the basket each year-end and held one year
result: Oppenheimer (1986): baskets bought each year-end 1970 to 1982 and held one year returned a mean 29.4%/yr vs 11.5% for the NYSE-AMEX index. Qualifiers are mostly tiny, illiquid stocks; few US names qualify today.

name: Inspired by Graham: Defensive Investor Screen
src: Benjamin Graham, 'The Intelligent Investor' (1949; criteria from the 4th rev. ed., 1973, ch. 14)
thesis: A mechanical quality-value checklist protects the amateur: size, financial strength, earnings stability, dividends, and a sane price.
criteria: Size: at least $100M annual sales for an industrial (1973 dollars)
Current ratio at least 2; long-term debt no more than net current assets
Some earnings each of past 10 years; EPS up at least one-third over 10 years (3-year averages)
Dividends paid each of past 20 years
Price at most 15x average 3-year earnings and 1.5x book, or P/E x P/B at most 22.5
result: Graham offered the screen as a safety standard and published no backtest. Tests of the exact seven rules are scarce, and results depend on how the size, 10-year and 20-year history tests are adapted.
run_gap: Applies 2 of Graham's 7 tests (the P/E and P/B caps); size, balance sheet, earnings and dividend record are not tested.

name: Inspired by Fama and French: Value Factor (HML)
src: Fama & French (1992, 1993), JF/JFE
thesis: High book-to-market stocks earn a premium over low book-to-market stocks not explained by beta.
criteria: Book equity (prior fiscal year) / market equity (December)
Each June: 2 size groups (NYSE median) x 3 B/M groups (NYSE 30th/70th pct)
HML = value-weighted high-B/M minus low-B/M, averaged across size; hold 12 months
result: HML averaged 0.40% per month (about 4.8%/yr, t = 2.91) from July 1963 to December 1991. Value then had a long drawdown from about 2007 to 2020, with a partial recovery since.
run_gap: Long only, the 30 highest book-to-market names; HML is a long-short factor across the top and bottom 30%.

name: Inspired by Greenblatt: Magic Formula
src: Joel Greenblatt, 'The Little Book That Beats the Market' (2005)
thesis: Rank the market on cheapness (earnings yield) plus quality (return on capital); buy the best combined ranks mechanically.
criteria: Earnings yield = EBIT / EV; return on capital = EBIT / (net working capital + net fixed assets)
Exclude utilities, financials and foreign stocks; apply a market-cap floor
Sum the two ranks; buy the top 20-30 in batches; hold each about one year
result: Book backtest: 30.8%/yr vs 12.4% for the S&P 500, 1988-2004, on the largest 3,500 US stocks. Independent tests (e.g. Gray and Carlisle, 2012) find it beat the market by less, with EBIT/EV alone doing better and multi-year droughts.
run_gap: Ranks on earnings yield (net income over market cap) with an ROE floor; Greenblatt sums ranks of EBIT/EV and return on capital.

name: Piotroski F-Score
src: Piotroski (2000), Journal of Accounting Research
thesis: Within cheap (high B/M) stocks, nine simple accounting signals separate the recovering from the dying.
criteria: Universe: highest book-to-market quintile
Score 0-9: ROA>0, CFO>0, rising ROA, CFO>ROA, lower leverage, higher current ratio, no equity issue, higher gross margin, higher asset turnover
Buy F-Score 8-9; F-Score 0-1 is the avoid or short group
result: 1976-1996: high F-Score (8-9) value stocks beat the average high-B/M stock by at least 7.5%/yr; long high minus short low (0-1) earned 23%/yr. Gains concentrate in small, thinly traded names with no analyst coverage.
run_gap: Liquid stocks only, 8 of the 9 signals, re-formed monthly; the paper found the effect in small, thinly traded firms held a year.

name: Inspired by Lakonishok, Shleifer and Vishny: Contrarian Value
src: Lakonishok, Shleifer & Vishny (1994), Journal of Finance
thesis: Value works because investors extrapolate past growth too far: low-priced, slow-growth stocks beat glamour stocks, and the gap is not explained by higher risk.
criteria: Sort NYSE/AMEX stocks each April on C/P, E/P or B/M and on 5-year sales growth
Value = high C/P and low growth; glamour = the reverse
Equal weight, buy and hold 5 years
result: Value beat glamour by about 10 to 11%/yr over the 5 years after formation in their 1968-1990 sample, and did not do worse in down markets or recessions.
run_gap: Mixes P/B, one quarter's sales growth and E/P in 30 names; the paper crosses one value ratio with 5-year sales growth.

name: Inspired by Carlisle: The Acquirer's Multiple
src: Tobias Carlisle, 'Deep Value' (2014) and 'The Acquirer's Multiple' (2017)
thesis: Carlisle argues cheapness alone (EV / operating earnings) beats the Magic Formula because high returns on capital tend to mean-revert, so the quality rank adds little.
criteria: Acquirer's Multiple = enterprise value / operating earnings (EBIT)
Buy the 30 lowest multiples above a market-cap floor, equal weight
Rebalance annually; expect ugly holdings
result: In a study Carlisle commissioned (1973-2017, 30 stocks), it beat the Magic Formula by about 0.3 to 2.4 points a year depending on the cap floor, and both beat the S&P 500. Author-run tests; long losing stretches occur.
run_gap: Ranks on net income over market cap, not enterprise value over operating earnings, and keeps financials.

name: Inspired by O'Shaughnessy: What Works on Wall Street
src: James O'Shaughnessy, 'What Works on Wall Street' (1996, 4th ed. 2011)
thesis: Decades of factor tests distilled: combined value composites (P/S, P/E, EV/EBITDA, P/CF, yield) beat any single ratio.
criteria: Value Composite: average rank on P/B, P/E, P/S, EBITDA/EV, P/CF and shareholder yield
Take the cheapest 10% of All Stocks by the composite
Buy the 25 with the best 6-month price gain; equal weight; rebalance annually
result: Trending Value compounded about 21%/yr from 1964 to 2009 in the 4th edition's backtest (before costs), well ahead of the All Stocks universe, with deep drawdowns along the way.
run_gap: Loose value caps, then a momentum rank: closer to momentum with a value floor than his six-ratio composite.

name: CAPE / Shiller P/E Timing
src: Campbell & Shiller (1988, 1998)
thesis: The cyclically-adjusted P/E (10-year real earnings) forecasts 10-year index returns - valuation matters at decade horizons.
criteria: CAPE (P/E10) = real S&P price / 10-year average real earnings
Used as a 10-year return forecast; the papers give no trading rule
An allocation tilt (less equity in top CAPE deciles) is our extension
result: Campbell and Shiller (1998) found P/E10 forecast 10-year real price changes in US data back to 1871, but not earnings growth; power at 1-year horizons is weak. CAPE stayed above its long-run mean for most of 1990-2020, so timing rules were often under-invested.

name: Inspired by Schloss: Cheap-Asset Basket
src: Walter Schloss letters & interviews; Buffett's 'Superinvestors' (1984)
thesis: Buy many statistically cheap stocks trading below book value and near multi-year lows, with little debt; rely on the balance sheet, not the story.
criteria: Price near multi-year low and below book (tangible book preferred)
Little or no debt, long operating history
Wide diversification (often about 100 names), about 4-year average hold
result: Buffett (1984): 16.1%/yr to limited partners vs 8.4% for the S&P, 1956-1984 (21.3%/yr before Schloss's share). Commonly cited 47-year record: about 15.3%/yr net vs about 10% for the S&P. A discretionary record, not a tested rule.
run_gap: Schloss used judgment, not a rule; this is a cheap-asset screen in his spirit, with no debt test.

name: Low Price-Earnings Portfolios
src: Sanjay Basu (1977), Journal of Finance
thesis: Rank stocks by price relative to reported earnings and favor the lowest P/E group. This is a direct earnings-yield value screen rather than a forecast of earnings growth.
criteria: NYSE industrials with December fiscal years; P/E = year-end price / annual EPS
Sort into P/E quintiles each April 1 (3-month reporting lag)
Buy the lowest-P/E quintile, hold 12 months, re-form yearly
result: April 1957 to March 1971: low-P/E portfolios earned higher raw and risk-adjusted returns than high-P/E portfolios, with returns falling roughly in order of P/E.
run_gap: The 30 lowest P/E names re-formed monthly, against Basu's yearly quintiles of NYSE industrials.

name: High Book-to-Market Stocks
src: Dennis Stattman (1980), The Chicago MBA: A Journal of Selected Papers
thesis: Use book equity relative to market capitalization to identify stocks priced cheaply relative to accounting net worth. Hold the higher book-to-market stocks rather than the lower book-to-market stocks.
criteria: Obtain book equity from the latest available financial statements.
Divide book equity by market capitalization for each eligible stock.
Form a portfolio from the highest book-to-market group and rebalance after accounting data update.
result: Stattman reported that US stocks with higher book-to-market earned higher average returns; Fama and French (1992) cite it with Rosenberg, Reid and Lanstein (1985) as early evidence of the value effect.
run_gap: A generic high book-to-market book; the source's own portfolio rules could not be checked.

name: Inspired by Dreman: Contrarian Low-P/E
src: David N. Dreman, 'Contrarian Investment Strategy' (1979)
thesis: Buy companies that the market values at depressed multiples, especially low P/E, while avoiding a fashionable consensus-growth approach. The approach is explicitly contrarian and emphasizes diversification.
criteria: Buy from the low-P/E group of medium and large companies
Require a sound balance sheet (low debt, adequate liquidity)
Diversify across many stocks and industries; sell as the P/E nears the market's
result: Dreman compiled evidence that unpopular low-P/E stocks beat glamour stocks over the periods he studied; he stresses that single holdings can be volatile. No single backtest figure is given here.
run_gap: The 30 lowest P/E re-formed monthly, with no size or financial-strength test; Dreman held for years.

name: Dogs of the Dow
src: Michael B. O'Higgins and John Downes, Beating the Dow (1991)
thesis: Among the Dow Jones Industrial Average constituents, high dividend yield is used as a simple proxy for temporarily depressed prices. Hold the ten highest-yielding Dow stocks for a year.
criteria: At each year-end, list the current Dow Jones Industrial Average constituents.
Rank them by indicated annual dividend divided by share price.
Buy the ten highest-yielding names in equal weights and rebalance annually.
result: The book reported the Dow 10 beat the Dow in its 1973-1991 tests. McQueen, Shields and Thorley (1997): 1946-1995 mean 16.77%/yr vs 13.71% for the Dow 30, with higher volatility; after risk, costs and taxes the edge was not significant.

name: International Book-to-Market Value
src: Eugene F. Fama and Kenneth R. French (1998), Journal of Finance
thesis: Apply value sorting outside the United States using book-to-market, earnings-to-price, cash-flow-to-price, and dividend yield. Compare high-value portfolios with low-value portfolios within international markets.
criteria: 13 major markets, MSCI data, 1975-1995
Within each country: value = top 30% by B/M (also E/P, C/P, D/P), growth = bottom 30%
Compare value minus growth, re-formed yearly
result: Global high-minus-low B/M returns averaged 7.68%/yr in 1975-1995, and value beat growth in 12 of 13 major markets; a value premium also appeared in emerging markets. Premiums vary widely by country and period.

name: High R&D-to-Market-Value Stocks
src: Louis K. C. Chan, Josef Lakonishok, and Theodore Sougiannis (2001), Journal of Finance
thesis: R&D is expensed, so R&D-heavy firms look worse on earnings and book value than their economics. The market appears too pessimistic about beaten-down R&D-intensive stocks.
criteria: Measure R&D intensity as R&D expense / market value of equity
Rank stocks on R&D-to-market; high values tend to follow poor past returns
Buy the highest group; firms with R&D earn no premium on average
result: Firms with R&D earned about the same average returns as firms without; firms with high R&D relative to market value earned large excess returns; R&D intensity went with higher return volatility.

name: Low Enterprise Multiple
src: Tim Loughran and Jay W. Wellman (2011), Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis
thesis: Value companies using enterprise value relative to EBITDA, which incorporates debt and cash as well as equity price. Favor the lower enterprise-multiple firms.
criteria: EV = equity market value + debt + preferred stock - cash
Divide by trailing EBITDA (positive values)
Rank on EV/EBITDA; hold the lowest-multiple group, rebalance periodically
result: An enterprise-multiple factor built Fama-French style earned a 5.28%/yr premium, July 1963 to December 2009; low-EM firms had higher later returns.
not_runnable: Our data has no enterprise value yet, so this cannot be run as published.

name: Inspired by Novy-Marx: Profitable Value
src: Robert Novy-Marx (2013), Journal of Financial Economics
thesis: Combine a conventional value screen with gross profitability, because profitable firms can be attractive even when their book-to-market alone does not identify them. The combination avoids treating all cheap firms as equivalent.
criteria: Calculate book-to-market using accounting book equity and market capitalization.
Calculate gross profitability as gross profits divided by total assets.
Select stocks that are relatively high in book-to-market and gross profitability, then rebalance on a stated schedule.
result: Gross profits-to-assets predicted returns about as well as book-to-market, and profitable firms outperformed despite higher valuations. Controlling for profitability sharply improved value strategies, especially among the largest, most liquid stocks.
run_gap: An ROE floor, then a P/B rank; the paper ranks gross profits over assets plus book-to-market, long-short.

name: Intangible-Adjusted Book-to-Market
src: Peters and Taylor (2017), JFE (intangible capital measure); return test: Eisfeldt, Kim and Papanikolaou (2022), Critical Finance Review
thesis: Add estimated intangible capital (capitalized R&D and part of SG&A) to book equity, since accounting book value omits it; rank on the adjusted book-to-market.
criteria: Knowledge capital: accumulate past R&D, net of depreciation
Organization capital: treat part of SG&A as investment (Peters-Taylor use 30%), depreciate yearly
Add both to book equity and rank on adjusted book-to-market
result: Peters and Taylor did not test returns: adding intangibles to q gives a stronger investment-q relation. Eisfeldt, Kim and Papanikolaou (2022) found an intangible-adjusted value factor earned substantially higher returns than standard HML, including in recent decades.

name: Inspired by Gray and Carlisle: Quantitative Value
src: Wesley R. Gray and Tobias E. Carlisle, Quantitative Value (2012)
thesis: Screen out likely manipulators and distressed firms, buy the cheapest stocks on EBIT / enterprise value, then keep the highest quality. The book tests many value ratios and picks EBIT/EV as the best single measure.
criteria: Drop firms flagged for earnings manipulation (accruals, M-score) or high distress risk
Take the cheapest decile by EBIT / total enterprise value
Keep the highest-quality names (franchise power + financial strength); equal weight, rebalance yearly
result: Book backtest 1974-2011: 17.68%/yr vs 10.46% for the S&P 500, about 3.7 points a year ahead of the Magic Formula. Author-run and before costs.
run_gap: Free cash flow over market cap instead of EBIT over enterprise value, and the quality step runs before the value step.
